newsitem.title: USA: Planning lessons from family business owners.
newsitem.headline: Planning lessons from family business owners.

text.p: A recent survey of veteran family business owners raises strategic planning issues that entrepreneurs in family-owned businesses should take to heart.

The survey, by the Arthur Andersen Centre for Family Business and the Massachusetts Mutual Life Insurance Co., found that nearly a third of the nation's family-owned businesses will experience leadership changes during the next five years.
The extent of advanced planning on turning over the reins to the next generation shows how even experienced business owners can ignore a critical issue.

The survey found that about 23 percent of senior generation shareholders had not completed any estate planning other than writing a will, and about a quarter of the respondents said significant shareholders do not know each other's estate plans and their intentions for transferring ownership and control of their companies.

"Management and ownership succession can be disruptive for any company, but it is particularly difficult in the context of the family relationships that exist in these businesses," said Ross Nager, executive director of the Arthur Andersen Centre for Family Business, in Houston.

With family-owned firms accounting for a majority of the nation's businesses, the smooth transition to new leadership is essential. "Their success in making this transition is critical not only to their owning families, but also to the health of our national economy," said Nager.

The 3,033 companies surveyed had combined revenues of $67.4 billion. The median company was 46 years old, with annual revenues of $9 million and 50 employees. The businesses are in a wide range of industries, with the four most common being manufacturing (24 percent), wholesale distribution (18 percent), retail (17 percent) and construction (14 percent).

Of the respondents, 37 percent were founders of the business and 41 percent were second-generation leaders, with only 18 percent representing third-generation CEOs. Ten percent of the companies reported having two CEOs, and 42 percent said it was possible that more than one family member would serve as co-CEO in the succeeding generation.

The survey found that less than a third of the companies had written strategic plans. Yet, it found that those with a written strategic plan tend to engage in other types of planning as well and generally tend to do better than those without.
Of those with strategic plans, 63 percent said that company management knows the plan "very well," while 35 percent said management knows the plan only "somewhat."

"The process of going through developing a plan forces the owner and family to focus on important issues," said Nager. "When you focus on those issues and discuss them, you are more likely to take actions which are healthy for the family and the business."

For example, he said, if in developing a strategic plan you decide it is important to keep the business in the family and that it continue to be recognised as a family-owned business, you must take concrete steps to keep it in the family.

Nager cites the need for a buy-sell agreement to restrict ownership legally should a family stockholder want to leave. It follows from that that the business and the family must plan how it will fund such an agreement.
"You also must start thinking about growth in the family," Nager said. "The business will need to support more family members. What do you need to do in order to make the business grow?"
While growing the business would likely already be the focus of a company business plan, providing for new family employees may be almost as daunting a task.

Basic questions to consider, said Nager, are: "Under what terms, if any, will we let family members come to work here? Will we let every family member come in, even if we don't have jobs available? Or will we require that there be a position, and that the family member be qualified for that position?"

Once these issues are worked out and a plan is developed, the plan must be communicated to the family and to key managers. "If the plan is just in the founder's head, it's not too likely the family and key managers will support and buy into it," Nager said.
He emphasises that the strategic plan should consider not only business issues, but also issues where the business and the family interact.
For example, while most businesses need capital to grow, family-owned businesses often need capital to pay estate taxes or to buy out departing shareholders. From where will the funds come?

In a family business, the death of an owner typically causes the business to have to come up with the capital to pay the estate taxes. Most people use life insurance for this purpose, but it is not always sufficient.

"Insurance tends to be fixed in amount, and we're talking about companies that continue to grow," said Nager. To keep coverage up to date, the company's valuation should be monitored and the amount of coverage adjusted .
Insurance is one tactic for dealing with the estate tax issue. But you need additional tactics too, such as trusts and gifting.

For example, the survey found that 43 percent of the business owners were not using their $10,000 tax-free annual gift exclusion, and only 23 percent had used the $600,000 per donor gift exclusion for reducing the value of their estates and lowering their estate taxes.

It's very difficult for most business owners to sit down and think about estate planning or an overall strategic plan because they're fighting fires all the time. Even if they do take the time to plan, planning by itself doesn't solve anything.
"You have to sit down and figure out the tactics, and then how to implement them," said Nager. "Time passes, and before ypu know it, the problems have gotten worse, and are tougher to deal with."
